hints: `read_excel("invoices.xlsx")` (from analyticskit) picks an engine the browser has — pandas' own `pd.read_excel` would ask for openpyxl.
problems.prompt:
`invoices.xlsx` is a workbook, not a CSV: it needs a spreadsheet reader: `read_excel` from `analyticskit`, which is imported for you (the in-browser Python reads .xlsx with python-calamine, not openpyxl).

Read it into `data` and print `data.shape`.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import read_excel

data = read_excel("invoices.xlsx")
print(data.shape)
problems.test_summary: Checks the eight columns and that all 5,000 invoices loaded.
problems.tests:
assert list(data.columns) == ["InvoiceID", "Date", "PartName", "Model", "Quantity", "Price", "Amount", "High Price"], f"unexpected columns: {list(data.columns)}"
assert len(data) == 5000
problems.title: Open the invoices workbook

problems.prompt:
Load `invoices.xlsx` into `data` and print the **median** of the `Amount` column, rounded to two decimals.

Compare it with `.mean()`: which one does the maximum pull away?
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import read_excel

data = read_excel("invoices.xlsx")
print(round(data["Amount"].median(), 2))
problems.test_summary: Checks the median is $1,949.87 and the maximum really is an outlier.
problems.tests:
assert round(float(data["Amount"].median()), 2) == 1949.87, f"median should be 1949.87, got {data['Amount'].median()}"
assert data["Amount"].max() > 1_000_000, "the maximum is an outlier"
problems.title: The median invoice is bigger than you think

hints: `data.PartName.value_counts()` sorts the counts from high to low.
The first entry is the winner: `counts.index[0]`.
problems.prompt:
Load `invoices.xlsx` into `data`.

Use `value_counts()` on `PartName` to find the part that appears most often, store that table in `counts`, and print the name of the top part.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import read_excel

data = read_excel("invoices.xlsx")
counts = data.PartName.value_counts()
print(counts.index[0])
problems.test_summary: Checks the most common part is Mouse and that it beats the runner-up.
problems.tests:
assert counts.index[0] == "Mouse", f"expected Mouse, got {counts.index[0]}"
assert counts.iloc[0] > counts.iloc[1], "the winner must beat the runner-up"
problems.title: Which part do people buy most?

hints: `data['Date'].dt.month` gives the month number for every row.
`.idxmax()` returns the label with the largest value.
problems.prompt:
Load `invoices.xlsx` into `data`.

Add a `month` column (`data.Date.dt.month`), group by it and take the maximum `Amount` per month. Print the month number whose maximum is the largest.
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import read_excel

data = read_excel("invoices.xlsx")
data["month"] = data.Date.dt.month
monthly = data.groupby("month")["Amount"].max()
print(monthly.idxmax())
problems.test_summary: Checks the grouped maximum points at July.
problems.tests:
assert int(data["month"].max()) <= 12
assert int(monthly.idxmax()) == 7, f"July has the spike, got {monthly.idxmax()}"
problems.title: Find the month with the biggest invoice

hints: `value_counts()` on an id column counts how many line items each invoice has.
problems.prompt:
Load `invoices.xlsx` into `data`, add the `month` column, and keep the July rows whose `Amount` is above `10,000` in a DataFrame called `july`.

Print `july['InvoiceID'].value_counts().index[0]` — the invoice number that stands out.

Then look at its quantities: are they plausible for a single order?
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import read_excel

data = read_excel("invoices.xlsx")
data["month"] = data.Date.dt.month
july = data[(data.month == 7) & (data.Amount > 10000)]

print(july["InvoiceID"].value_counts().index[0])
problems.test_summary: Checks the July filter and that the flagged invoice has several large line items.
problems.tests:
assert len(july) > 0
assert july["Amount"].min() > 10000
assert july["InvoiceID"].value_counts().iloc[0] >= 4, "the odd invoice has several line items"
problems.title: Investigate the July bulk order

hints: The mean of a column of zeros and ones is the proportion of ones.
`.mean()` ignores nothing here — every row has a value.
problems.prompt: `High Price` is a 0/1 column. Fill in the blanks so the cell prints the share of rows that are high price, formatted as a percentage with two decimals (`18.00%`).
problems.solution:
import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import read_excel

data = read_excel("invoices.xlsx")
share = data["High Price"].mean()
print(f"{share:.2%}")

import pandas as pd
from analyticskit import read_excel

data = read_excel("invoices.xlsx")
share = data["High Price"].___(0.18)

problems.tests: assert abs(float(data["High Price"].mean()) - 0.18) < 0.001, "about 18% of invoices are high price"
